title: Units of Measure and Metric Conversions

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify metric units of measure for weight, volume, length, and temperature.
- Convert accurately within the metric system, including gram, milligram, microgram, liter, and milliliter conversions.
- Apply household-to-metric equivalencies for common measurements.
- Recognize the safety importance of correct units, decimal placement, and error-prone abbreviations.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Grams are like the 'scoop size' we use to describe how heavy something is. Liters describe how much space a liquid takes up, and meters describe how long something is.

### Question 2

A liter is like a big bottle of water. It tells you how much room a liquid takes up, not how heavy it is.

### Question 3

If you cut a sandwich into 1,000 tiny pieces, each piece is one 'milli' piece. A milligram is a gram cut into 1,000 equal pieces.

### Question 4

A kilogram is like 1,000 little gram blocks all stuck together into one big block.

### Question 5

A microgram is unbelievably small — like one tiny grain of sand compared to a whole bucket of sand (a gram).

### Question 6

'mcg' with a 'c' in the middle means the super-small unit. 'mg' without the 'c' is the bigger unit (milligram).

### Question 7

'mg' means milligram — a gram cut into 1,000 pieces.

### Question 8

Imagine four buckets: a huge one (kg), a big one (g), a cup (mg), and a thimble (mcg). Biggest to smallest is bucket, big, cup, thimble.

### Question 9

If a gram is a whole pizza, a milligram is one crumb of it, and a microgram is a speck of dust next to the crumb. The speck is smallest.

### Question 10

A milliliter and a cubic centimeter are two names for the exact same little box of space.

### Question 11

A milligram is 1,000 times smaller than a gram, so half a gram turns into 500 of those smaller pieces.

### Question 12

If a gram is cut into 1,000 pieces, 250 of those pieces is the same as one-quarter (0.25) of the whole gram.

### Question 13

Two whole grams is the same as 2,000 little milligram pieces.

### Question 14

A microgram is 1,000 times smaller than a milligram, so 0.125 mg expands into 125 of those tiny pieces.

### Question 15

If 1,000 micrograms make one milligram, then 400 micrograms is a little less than half of one milligram (0.4 mg).

### Question 16

One and a half kilograms is the same as 1,500 grams.

### Question 17

0.05 of a gram is five-hundredths of a gram, which is the same as 50 milligrams.

### Question 18

One-tenth of a milligram is the same as 100 micrograms.

### Question 19

A gram is a million micrograms — like a million tiny grains of sand making one full scoop.

### Question 20

Going from kilograms all the way down to milligrams means jumping two steps of 1,000, which is like multiplying by a million.

### Question 21

750 milligrams is three-quarters of a gram, written as 0.75 grams.

### Question 22

600 micrograms is a little more than half of one milligram, which is 0.6 mg.

### Question 23

Two and a half grams is the same as 2,500 milligrams.

### Question 24

Exactly 1,000 microgram pieces stack up to make one single milligram.

### Question 25

Two-hundredths of a gram (0.02 g) is the same as 20 milligrams.

### Question 26

Five whole grams equals 5,000 milligrams.

### Question 27

Three-quarters of a gram (0.75 g) is the same as 750 milligrams.

### Question 28

One and two-tenths grams (1.2 g) equals 1,200 milligrams.

### Question 29

Ten milligrams is the same as 10,000 micrograms — the number gets 1,000 times bigger when you switch to the tiny unit.

### Question 30

Half a liter is the same as 500 milliliters — like half a big water bottle.

### Question 31

750 milliliters is three-quarters of a liter, written as 0.75 L.

### Question 32

Two full liters is the same as 2,000 milliliters.

### Question 33

250 milliliters is one-quarter of a liter, written as 0.25 L.

### Question 34

Five-hundredths of a liter (0.05 L) is the same as 50 milliliters.

### Question 35

One and a half liters is the same as 1,500 milliliters.

### Question 36

125 milliliters is one-eighth of a liter, written as 0.125 L.

### Question 37

One-hundredth of a liter (0.01 L) is the same as 10 milliliters.

### Question 38

Three and two-tenths liters (3.2 L) is the same as 3,200 milliliters.

### Question 39

Six-tenths of a liter (0.6 L) is the same as 600 milliliters.

### Question 40

A milliliter and a cubic centimeter are the same size, so the number does not change at all.

### Question 41

One liter is like a big bottle that can be poured into 1,000 tiny milliliter cups.

### Question 42

A teaspoon is a small spoon that holds about 5 little milliliter units of liquid.

### Question 43

A tablespoon is the bigger spoon that holds about three times as much as a teaspoon — about 15 milliliters.

### Question 44

Two big spoonfuls (tablespoons) make about 30 milliliters.

### Question 45

A fluid ounce is about 30 milliliters — think of a small medicine cup.

### Question 46

A full measuring cup holds about 240 milliliters, which is the same as 8 fluid ounces.

### Question 47

A cup holds 8 fluid ounces — like eight little one-ounce medicine cups poured together.

### Question 48

A kilogram is a little more than two pounds — like a bag of flour that weighs about 2.2 pounds.

### Question 49

An inch is a little more than two and a half centimeters.

### Question 50

Three little spoons (teaspoons) pour exactly into one big spoon (tablespoon).

### Question 51

Fifteen milliliters is one big spoonful (tablespoon).

### Question 52

Ten milliliters is two small spoonfuls (teaspoons), since each teaspoon is about 5 milliliters.

### Question 53

A pound is 16 ounces — like 16 little one-ounce blocks stacked together.

### Question 54

A pint is two cups poured together, which is about 480 milliliters.

### Question 55

Two one-ounce medicine cups full is 60 milliliters.

### Question 56

Four fluid ounces is half a cup, which is 120 milliliters.

### Question 57

Putting a zero in front of the dot is like putting a big warning sign that says 'the dot is coming!' so nobody misses it.

### Question 58

Writing '5.0' is risky because the dot and zero can blend together and look like '50.' Better to just write plain '5.'

### Question 59

If the dot is missing, '.5' can look like just '5.' Writing '0.5' makes the little dot impossible to miss.

### Question 60

The letter 'U' can look like a '0,' so we write the whole word 'units' so nobody adds an extra zero by mistake.

### Question 61

We write 'mL' because it is clear. The old 'cc' could be mistaken for '00' (zeros), which would change the amount.

### Question 62

The squiggly Greek letter can look like an 'm,' which would turn a tiny microgram into a milligram — a thousand times too much. 'mcg' is safer to read.

### Question 63

Moving the dot one spot is like multiplying or dividing by 10 — it turns 0.5 into 5, which is ten times bigger.

### Question 64

The dot in '5.0' can hide, and '5.0' can start to look like '50.' That is why we never add that extra zero.

### Question 65

A milligram is like a whole bowl of cereal, while a microgram is one single flake. Confusing the bowl for the flake is a gigantic mistake.

### Question 66

When you cannot tell if a number is big or small, you ask the person in charge instead of guessing — just like checking with a teacher before guessing on a test.

### Question 67

Five-tenths means half, and we write '0.5' so the dot can never be missed.

### Question 68

A capital 'U' can look like a zero, and '10U' could turn into '100.' Writing 'units' avoids that mix-up.

### Question 69

The fancy Greek letter at the start can look like an 'm,' turning a tiny microgram into a much bigger milligram.

### Question 70

Leaving off the zero in front of the dot is the number-one way a half turns into a five — ten times too much.

### Question 71

Copy the label exactly — same number, same unit — like copying a recipe without changing any ingredient amounts.

### Question 72

Two sets of eyes are better than one — like having a friend check your math homework before you turn it in.

### Question 73

Use the scale's 'kilograms' setting and write down exactly what it says, so every weight is measured the same way.

### Question 74

When you are not sure which size of cup to use, ask the person in charge instead of picking one yourself.

### Question 75

Since each kilogram is a little more than two pounds, a 154-pound person weighs about 70 kilograms.

### Question 76

A 110-pound weight is exactly 50 kilograms, since 50 kilograms times 2.2 is 110 pounds.

### Question 77

220 pounds divided by 2.2 is exactly 100 kilograms — a nice round number to remember.

### Question 78

Each inch is about 2.5 centimeters, so 60 inches makes about 152 centimeters.

### Question 79

Weights are written in kilograms, like saying a person weighs '70 kilograms' instead of '154 pounds.'

### Question 80

A medicine syringe measures how much liquid it holds, and liquids are measured in milliliters.

### Question 81

We write a child's height in centimeters, like '120 cm,' just like a ruler marked in centimeters.

### Question 82

It tells us how many little milligram units of a substance are swimming in each small cup (deciliter) of the fluid.

### Question 83

Half of one milliliter is '0.5 mL' — the zero in front keeps the little dot from being missed.

### Question 84

A quarter of a milligram is 250 micrograms — the number gets 1,000 times bigger when we switch to the tiny unit.

### Question 85

500 milligrams is half a gram, written as 0.5 grams.

### Question 86

We pour every drink into the same-size mental measuring cup (milliliters) so we can add them all up correctly.

### Question 87

98.6 degrees Fahrenheit is the same 'just right' body warmth as 37 degrees Celsius.

### Question 88

Some jobs are for the doctor or nurse only. When someone asks about medicine amounts, the helper's job is to hand that question to the right person.

### Question 89

If you are not sure how to change pounds into kilograms, use a trustworthy way to convert it or ask a co-worker to double-check — never just guess.
